summary.title: How I Write Tests
summary.one_liner: A practitioner's approach to testing without strict test-first rules: write module and tests together, avoid manual runs, build fakes, miniformats and data-driven test "zoos", and turn every bug into a regression test.
takeaways: Write each module and its tests together before moving on, keeping modules testable and minimally coupled rather than writing tests strictly first.
Replace manual, run-the-binary testing with automated tests, since manual checks only validate the current code state.
Build reusable fakes for external dependencies instead of ad-hoc stubs, and small human-readable textual formats for test inputs and outputs.
Consider a data-driven 'zoo' test harness where new test cases are just data files, as compiler projects like GCC do.
Encode every bug found as a regression test to ratchet down the set of possible failures over time.
summary.summary: Nelson Hage describes his personal testing philosophy, which he sees as a loose form of test-driven development without strict test-first rules. He works module by module, designing for testability with few dependencies, and resists manual testing in favor of automated tests. The post then covers concrete techniques: reusable in-memory or programmable fakes (with examples from Django, the sarama Go Kafka client), small textual miniformats for test data (David Benjamin's DER ASCII), data-driven "zoo" test harnesses (illustrated with GCC's test suite), and writing regression tests for every bug found.
